title: Reading & Use of English
paragraphs: My name is Aigerim Bekova. I am twenty-five years old and I work as a programme coordinator at GlobalAid, an international non-governmental organisation based in Almaty. I came to WKU in Uralsk to study International Relations, and it was there that I began seriously learning English. Over the past two years, while working full-time, I have completed all twenty-six modules of the B1 English course. It has not been easy, but it has been worth it.

When I started the course, my English was functional but limited. I could send basic emails and understand instructions, but I could not have a substantive conversation about ideas, or write an argument that I was genuinely proud of. My work at GlobalAid involves coordinating between local teams and international partners — organisations from Europe, North America, and East Asia. In practice, this means that English is not just a skill for me but a tool I use every single working day.

The twenty-six modules of the course have taken me through territory I had not expected to cover: not just grammar and vocabulary, but questions about society, technology, the environment, and work. In the modules on society, I learned vocabulary and frameworks for thinking about inequality, social mobility, and civic responsibility. In the modules on technology, I studied how digital tools are reshaping communication, education, and employment — including in organisations like the one I work for. The environment modules gave me language for discussing climate change, resource management, and the obligations that individuals and institutions share. The modules on work helped me understand the formal and semi-formal registers that professional English requires.

The grammar modules were harder than I expected. I had always thought my grammar was adequate — and in some areas it was. But the course pushed me into territory I had avoided: complex conditionals, the passive in all its forms, the precise use of articles, reported speech in formal contexts, comparatives and hedging in academic writing. By the time I completed the final grammar review, I realised that what I had called "adequate" was actually "functional but imprecise." There is a real difference between the two, especially in professional contexts where clarity matters.

The aspect of the course that surprised me most was the writing. I had expected writing tasks to be difficult. What I had not expected was how much a structured approach to writing would change the way I thought. Learning to plan arguments, to acknowledge counter-arguments before rebutting them, to use formal framing phrases and discourse markers purposefully — these are not just writing skills. They are thinking skills. I find now that I plan my English emails more carefully, structure my reports more clearly, and express my reasoning more precisely than I did before.

If I had to identify the single most important thing the course gave me, it would not be a specific grammar point or a piece of vocabulary. It would be confidence — the confidence that comes from knowing you have genuinely worked at something and improved. That confidence changes how I speak in meetings, how I respond to emails from international partners, and how I present at conferences. It is not the confidence of thinking you are perfect. It is the confidence of knowing that you have the tools to communicate clearly and that, when things go wrong, you have the strategies to repair them.

I am not finished. The course has brought me to B1 and opened the door to B2. The work ahead — more complex reading, more sophisticated writing, more demanding conversations — is still substantial. But I know now that it is possible. And I know that the same approach that got me through twenty-six modules — sustained, deliberate engagement, week after week — is what will take me further. The language develops through use. I have learned that, and I intend to put it into practice.

dialogue.speaker: Colleague
dialogue.text: Aigerim, your presentations in English have really improved this year. What changed?

dialogue.speaker: Aigerim
dialogue.text: I completed a structured B1 course — twenty-six modules, over two years. It was demanding alongside full-time work, but it changed how I think in English, not just how I speak it.

dialogue.speaker: Colleague
dialogue.text: Which part helped you most professionally?

dialogue.speaker: Aigerim
dialogue.text: The writing modules. I thought I could write adequately before. What the course showed me was that "adequate" and "precise" are very different things — especially in formal contexts.

dialogue.speaker: Colleague
dialogue.text: What would you say to someone thinking of doing something similar?

dialogue.speaker: Aigerim
dialogue.text: Start, and don't stop. The progress is slow at first. But sustained, deliberate engagement — week after week — is what produces real development. There are no shortcuts.

keyPhrases.context: A conversation that engages with real ideas and arguments, not just basic exchange.
Working well enough for basic purposes but lacking the precision needed for formal contexts.
Words and phrases that organise text and signal logical relationships: "however", "therefore", "crucially".
Using language carefully to avoid overstating claims: "suggests", "may", "appears to".
Regular, purposeful practice as the most reliable predictor of language development.
The level of formality appropriate to a context — formal, semi-formal, or informal.
The duties and obligations that members of society have towards each other and their communities.
The careful and efficient use of natural or institutional resources.

vocab.definition: having real, meaningful content; not trivial or superficial
vocab.example: "I could not have a substantive conversation about ideas." — meaningful, not just basic.

vocab.definition: to organise different people or groups so they work together effectively
vocab.example: "My work involves coordinating between local teams and international partners."

vocab.definition: relating to a city or town, or the duties of citizens
vocab.example: "The society modules covered civic responsibility and participation."

vocab.definition: to change the shape, structure, or nature of something significantly
vocab.example: "Technology is reshaping communication, education, and employment."

vocab.definition: the quality of being exact and accurate
vocab.example: "There is a real difference between functional and precise English."

vocab.definition: to prove that a claim or argument is false; to counter an objection
vocab.example: "I learned to acknowledge counter-arguments before rebutting them."

vocab.definition: satisfactory or acceptable for a particular purpose, though not outstanding
vocab.example: "What I had called adequate was actually functional but imprecise."

vocab.definition: a duty or responsibility to do something
vocab.example: "The environment modules covered the obligations individuals and institutions share."

questions.text: "By the time I completed the final grammar review, I realised…" — What tense pattern is used here?
questions.hint: "Had completed" (Past Perfect) = completed before "I realised" (Past Simple). ✅

questions.text: "Technology is reshaping communication." — The tense here is:
questions.hint: "is reshaping" = Present Continuous — an ongoing, current process. ✅

questions.text: "If I had to identify the single most important thing, it would not be a specific grammar point." — This is:
questions.hint: "If + past simple, would + infinitive" = second conditional — hypothetical present. ✅

questions.text: "Sustained, deliberate engagement — week after week — is what will take me further." "Sustained" means:
questions.hint: "Sustained" = maintained continuously; not stopping.

questions.text: "___ working full-time, she completed all twenty-six modules." (concession — noun/gerund)
questions.hint: "Despite + gerund/noun" — no separate subject clause. ✅

questions.text: "___ she was working full-time, she completed all twenty-six modules." (concession — clause)
questions.hint: "Although + clause (subject + verb)." ✅

questions.text: "The results were striking. ___, the team published the report immediately."
questions.hint: Cause → effect: THEREFORE / AS A RESULT / CONSEQUENTLY. ✅

questions.text: "By the time she finishes the B2 course, she ___ English for over four years."
questions.hint: "By the time + present simple → future perfect: will have + pp." ✅

questions.text: "The report ___ (submit) to the partners last month." (Past Simple Passive)
questions.hint: "Was submitted" = Past Simple Passive. ✅

questions.text: "A new training programme ___ (develop) now for international staff." (ongoing now)
questions.hint: "Is being developed" = Present Continuous Passive. Ongoing now. ✅

questions.text: "She ___ (work) at GlobalAid for three years." (up to now — result matters)
questions.hint: Completed with present relevance → Present Perfect; duration → Present Perfect Continuous. ✅

questions.text: "She intended to focus ___ professional writing skills." Correct preposition:
questions.hint: "Intend to focus ON [topic]." ✅

questions.text: "All staff ___ respond to international partners within 48 hours." — "must respond" is:
questions.hint: "Must + infinitive (active)" = obligation. Not passive — no "be + pp." ✅

questions.text: "She told me that she ___ completing the course the following year." (reported speech)
questions.hint: Reported speech: present → past. "She intends" → "She told me she intended." ✅

questions.text: "What I had called adequate was actually functional but imprecise." "Adequate" means:
questions.hint: "adequate" = good enough for basic purposes; acceptable but not excellent.

questions.text: "Technology is reshaping communication." "Reshaping" means:
opts: Changing significantly in structure or character
questions.correct: Changing significantly in structure or character
questions.hint: "reshape" = to change the form or nature of something significantly.

questions.text: "I learned to acknowledge counter-arguments before rebutting them." "Rebutting" means:
questions.hint: "rebut" = to prove that an argument or claim is false.

questions.text: "There is a real difference between adequate and precise, especially where clarity matters." "Precision" means:
opts: The quality of being exact and accurate
questions.correct: The quality of being exact and accurate
questions.hint: "precision" = exactness and accuracy — the opposite of vagueness.

questions.text: "The environment modules covered the obligations individuals and institutions share." "Obligation" means:
questions.hint: "obligation" = a duty; something you are required to do.
